topics.tagline: Chatbots, chips and the trillion-dollar race everyone has an opinion on.
topics.why: Artificial intelligence went from a research topic to everyday life when ChatGPT launched in late 2022. Now it's in workplaces, phones and the stock market, and everyone talks about which tools they use, whether AI will take jobs, and how fast it's improving. You don't need to be technical; knowing the key players, terms and debates is enough to hold your own.

essentials.title: Large language models
essentials.body: Chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek run on large language models (LLMs): systems trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language.

essentials.title: Generative AI
essentials.body: AI that creates text, images, video, music and code. Tools like Midjourney and Sora make images and video from prompts.

essentials.title: Chips and compute
essentials.body: Training AI needs enormous computing power, mostly Nvidia chips in giant data centres. That's why Nvidia became the world's most valuable company.

essentials.title: The big labs
essentials.body: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta and xAI in the US; DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot and others in China. They race to release better models.

essentials.title: Agents are the next step
essentials.body: AI 'agents' can take actions on their own, like browsing, coding or booking, not just answering questions.

essentials.title: Risks and rules
essentials.body: Concerns include misinformation, deepfakes, job loss, bias and long-term safety. The EU passed an AI Act; other countries are writing rules.

topics.tagline: Art Basel, M+, auction records and how to talk about art without bluffing.
topics.why: Hong Kong is Asia's art market capital, home to Art Basel Hong Kong, the M+ museum and major auction houses. Art comes up at gallery openings, dinners and in news about record-breaking sales. You don't need an art history degree; knowing the major movements, famous names, local institutions and some useful vocabulary lets you enjoy and discuss art confidently.

essentials.title: Major movements
essentials.body: Renaissance (Leonardo, Michelangelo), Impressionism (Monet), Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh), Cubism (Picasso), Abstract Expressionism (Pollock, Rothko), Pop Art (Warhol) and Contemporary art.

essentials.title: Contemporary vs modern
essentials.body: Modern art is roughly 1860s to 1970s; contemporary art is from the 1970s to now.

essentials.title: The art market
essentials.body: Galleries sell new work (primary market); auction houses resell it (secondary market). Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips dominate auctions.

essentials.title: Art fairs
essentials.body: Art Basel (Basel, Miami, Hong Kong, Paris) and Frieze gather galleries from around the world.

essentials.title: Chinese and Asian art
essentials.body: From ancient ceramics and ink painting to modern masters like Zao Wou-Ki and Sanyu and contemporary stars like Ai Weiwei and Yayoi Kusama.

essentials.title: How to look at art
essentials.body: Ask what you notice, how it makes you feel, and what the artist might be saying. There's no wrong reaction.

topics.tagline: Horsepower, heritage, and the endless argument about manual gearboxes.
topics.why: Cars are the one hobby almost everyone has an opinion on. Car people bond over performance, design, nostalgia for the cars they grew up with, and big debates about where things are going: electric vs petrol, screens vs buttons, automatic vs manual. In Hong Kong cars are also a status statement because owning one is so expensive. You don't need to know engineering, just the vocabulary and the personalities of the brands.

essentials.title: Engines in plain words
essentials.body: People talk about cylinders (four, six, V8, V12), turbocharged vs naturally aspirated, and horsepower (top-end power) vs torque (pulling force).

essentials.title: Which wheels drive
essentials.body: FWD (front-wheel drive) is practical, RWD (rear-wheel drive) is the enthusiast's favourite, AWD (all-wheel drive) grips best in bad weather.

essentials.title: Powertrains
essentials.body: Petrol, diesel, hybrid (petrol plus battery), plug-in hybrid and fully electric (EV). Hybrids are booming as a middle ground.

essentials.title: Car cultures
essentials.body: JDM (Japanese), Euro (German and Italian), American muscle, off-road, exotics and supercars, EV fans. People usually belong to one tribe.

essentials.title: Brands have personalities
essentials.body: Porsche is precision, Ferrari is passion, Toyota is reliability, BMW is 'the ultimate driving machine', Mercedes is luxury, Tesla is tech, Volvo is safety.

essentials.title: Body styles
essentials.body: Saloon (sedan), hatchback, estate (wagon), coupe, convertible, SUV, MPV (people carrier). SUVs now dominate sales worldwide.

essentials.title: Everything is changing
essentials.body: Electrification, Chinese brands going global, and software-heavy cars are the big shifts car people talk about.

topics.tagline: From yuenyeung to pour-over: how coffee became Hong Kong's social glue.
topics.why: Coffee is the easiest small talk there is: almost everyone drinks it and has a favourite spot. Hong Kong has gone from instant coffee and cha chaan teng milk coffee to one of Asia's best specialty coffee scenes. Knowing the drinks, the brewing methods and a few local names lets you talk cafés, origins and trends with anyone.

essentials.title: Arabica vs robusta
essentials.body: Arabica beans are smoother and more aromatic, used in specialty coffee. Robusta is stronger, more bitter and has more caffeine.

essentials.title: Origins taste different
essentials.body: Ethiopian beans are often fruity and floral, Colombian balanced, Brazilian nutty and chocolatey, Indonesian earthy.

essentials.title: Roast level
essentials.body: Light roasts keep fruity origin flavours; dark roasts taste roasty and bitter. Specialty cafés favour light to medium.

essentials.title: Espresso drinks
essentials.body: Espresso is the base. Add hot water for an Americano, steamed milk for a latte or flat white, foam for a cappuccino.

essentials.title: Filter coffee
essentials.body: Pour-over (like V60), French press, AeroPress and cold brew bring out different flavours. Pour-over is the specialty café ritual.

essentials.title: Third wave
essentials.body: The 'third wave' treats coffee like wine: single origins, light roasts, careful brewing. First wave was instant; second was Starbucks.

topics.tagline: Bitcoin, wild price swings, and Hong Kong's push to be a crypto hub.
topics.why: Crypto went from a niche internet experiment to something Wall Street, governments and your colleagues talk about. Bitcoin is now held by ETFs and companies, stablecoins are being regulated, and Hong Kong has positioned itself as a licensed crypto hub. It's polarising: some see the future of money, others a casino. Knowing the basics lets you join in without being lost or preachy.

essentials.title: Bitcoin is digital gold
essentials.body: Created in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. Only 21 million will ever exist. Fans see it as a hedge against inflation and money printing.

essentials.title: Ethereum is a platform
essentials.body: Ethereum runs programs called smart contracts, which power stablecoins, DeFi and NFTs. Its coin is ether (ETH).

essentials.title: Stablecoins are crypto dollars
essentials.body: Coins like USDT (Tether) and USDC are pegged to the US dollar and used for trading and payments. They're now being regulated in the US and Hong Kong.

essentials.title: Prices are extremely volatile
essentials.body: Bitcoin has crashed more than 70% several times and recovered to new highs. Altcoins swing even more.

topics.tagline: The Tour de France, carbon bikes and the long cycle tracks of the New Territories.
topics.why: Cycling is both a huge pro sport, with the Tour de France as one of the world's biggest events, and a popular hobby for fitness, social rides and weekend adventures. topics.tagline: Who owns whom, who's designing where, and why 'quiet luxury' took over.
topics.why: Luxury fashion is a giant business run by a few conglomerates, and its gossip is about creative directors swapping houses, prices rising, and what's 'in'. In Hong Kong luxury shopping is part of the city's identity, from Central's flagships to Harbour City. Knowing the big houses, their designers and the current trends makes it easy to talk style without being a fashionista.

essentials.title: A few groups own most brands
essentials.body: LVMH (Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine, Loewe, Fendi, Tiffany), Kering (Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta, Balenciaga), Richemont (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, mostly jewellery and watches). Hermès and Chanel are independent and family-controlled.

essentials.title: Creative directors are the stars
essentials.body: Each house has a creative director who sets its look. When one moves, it's front-page news. 2025 saw a historic reshuffle at almost every major house.

essentials.title: The fashion calendar
essentials.body: Fashion weeks in New York, London, Milan and Paris twice a year show collections months ahead. Paris is the most important; haute couture is the hand-made top tier.

essentials.title: Logos vs quiet luxury
essentials.body: Fashion swings between loud logos (Gucci in the late 2010s) and 'quiet luxury', understated pieces without visible branding (Loro Piana, The Row, Brunello Cucinelli).

essentials.title: Prices keep rising
essentials.body: Luxury brands raised prices sharply after 2020. Some customers pushed back, and sales slowed in 2024-25, especially in China.

essentials.title: Streetwear and luxury merged
essentials.body: Supreme x Louis Vuitton (2017) and Virgil Abloh at Louis Vuitton made sneakers and hoodies part of luxury.

topics.why: Fitness is one of the most common things people talk about: their runs, gym routines, races and gadgets. Hong Kong has a big running and gym culture, from the Standard Chartered Marathon to Hyrox races and trail ultras. Knowing the training vocabulary, the big events and current trends lets you swap tips and encouragement with anyone.

essentials.title: Cardio vs strength
essentials.body: Cardio (running, cycling, swimming) builds endurance; strength training (weights) builds muscle and bone. Most experts recommend both.

essentials.title: Race distances
essentials.body: 5K, 10K, half marathon (21.1 km) and marathon (42.2 km). Anything longer is an ultramarathon.

essentials.title: The World Marathon Majors
essentials.body: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York and Sydney (added in 2025). Finishing all of them earns a 'six-star' (now seven-star) medal.

essentials.title: Zone 2 and heart rate
essentials.body: Training at an easy, conversational pace (zone 2) builds aerobic fitness. Many runners do most runs slow and a few fast.

essentials.title: Hybrid fitness
essentials.body: Hyrox, a race mixing running with functional workouts, exploded worldwide, including in Hong Kong.

essentials.title: Recovery matters
essentials.body: Sleep, rest days, protein and mobility work are as important as training.

topics.tagline: Twenty-two drivers, 11 teams, 24 races, and more politics than a royal court.
topics.why: Formula 1 is the top level of single-seater motor racing: the fastest circuit cars on earth, racing on a calendar that spans five continents from March to December. Netflix's Drive to Survive (2019 onward) and the 2025 Brad Pitt film F1 turned it into a mainstream obsession. Fans love the driver rivalries, the engineering arms race and the team drama as much as the racing itself.

essentials.title: Two championships at once
essentials.body: There's a Drivers' Championship and a Constructors' (teams') Championship. Each team runs two cars, so your teammate is your first rival: same car, no excuses.

essentials.title: The car matters enormously
essentials.body: Every team designs its own car. A great driver in a slow car rarely wins, which is why it's huge news when a star switches teams. People estimate the car is most of the performance.

essentials.title: How a race weekend works
essentials.body: Practice on Friday, Qualifying on Saturday to set the starting order, the Grand Prix on Sunday. Six weekends a year add a short Saturday Sprint race. Points go to the top 10: 25, 18, 15, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1.

essentials.title: Qualifying is a knockout
essentials.body: Q1 drops the slowest cars, Q2 drops more, and the fastest ten fight for pole position in Q3. On tracks like Monaco, qualifying decides the race.

essentials.title: Strategy is tyres and pit stops
essentials.body: Pirelli supplies soft, medium and hard tyres. In a dry race each car must use two different compounds, so everyone pits at least once. Stops take 2 to 3 seconds, and timing them well wins races.

essentials.title: Money and rules
essentials.body: The FIA writes the rules and Liberty Media owns the commercial side. A budget cap since 2021 limits spending so the rich teams can't simply outspend everyone.

essentials.title: 2026 reset the rules
essentials.body: Brand-new regulations arrived in 2026: smaller, lighter cars, movable wings, engines that get about half their power from electricity, and fully sustainable fuel. New rules usually reshuffle who's fast.

topics.tagline: Four majors, one tiny ball, and a sport that's half networking.
topics.why: Golf is both a pro sport with global superstars and a social and business ritual, especially in Hong Kong where club memberships are status symbols. Pro golf has been through a civil war since Saudi-backed LIV Golf launched in 2022. Even if you don't play, knowing the majors, the big names and a bit of vocabulary makes you fluent at the 19th hole.

essentials.title: How scoring works
essentials.body: Each hole has a 'par', the number of shots a good player should take (3, 4 or 5). A course is usually par 70-72. Fewer shots is better; '-10' means ten under par.

essentials.title: The four majors
essentials.body: The Masters (April, Augusta), the PGA Championship (May), the US Open (June) and The Open Championship (July, in the UK). Majors define careers.

essentials.title: Tournaments last four days
essentials.body: Pro events are 72 holes over Thursday to Sunday, with a 'cut' after day two that sends half the field home.

essentials.title: The PGA Tour vs LIV
essentials.body: In 2022 Saudi-funded LIV Golf lured stars with huge contracts. It split the sport; talks about a merger dragged on and the majors are where both sides meet.

essentials.title: The Ryder Cup
essentials.body: Europe vs the USA every two years, team match play with wild crowds. The most emotional event in golf. Europe won in 2023 and again away in New York in 2025.

essentials.title: Handicaps let everyone play together
essentials.body: Amateurs have a handicap showing roughly how many shots over par they shoot, so players of different abilities can compete.

topics.tagline: Dragon's Back, Lion Rock and the four great trails: Hong Kong's green secret.
topics.why: Most visitors don't realise that about 40% of Hong Kong is country park. Hiking is one of the city's favourite weekend activities, with dramatic peaks, beaches and trails minutes from skyscrapers. Hikers talk about routes, difficulty, views and the weather. Knowing the famous trails and some hiking lingo makes you great company and might get you invited along.

essentials.title: Country parks
essentials.body: Hong Kong has 25 country parks covering about 40% of its land, with well-marked trails and distance posts.

essentials.title: Famous hikes

essentials.title: Weather and safety
essentials.body: Heat, humidity and typhoons are serious. Check warnings, carry plenty of water, and avoid hiking in heavy rain or very hot weather.

topics.tagline: The world's most expensive homes, nano flats, and everyone's favourite topic.
topics.why: Property is Hong Kong's national obsession. Homes are among the most expensive on earth relative to income, so buying, renting, mortgages and prices come up at every family dinner. After years of falling prices since 2021, the market has been trying to find a bottom. Knowing the vocabulary, the big developers and the policy changes makes you fluent in the city's favourite small talk.

essentials.title: Extremely expensive
essentials.body: Hong Kong has topped global unaffordability rankings for years, with home prices many times the median household income.

essentials.title: Prices fell after 2021

essentials.title: Saleable area is what matters
essentials.body: Flats are measured in square feet, and since 2013 prices must be quoted by saleable area (actual usable space), not the inflated gross area.

essentials.title: Public vs private housing
essentials.body: About half the population lives in public rental housing or subsidised Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) flats. Waiting times for public housing are years long.

essentials.title: Policy moves the market
essentials.body: The government removed all the 'spicy' extra stamp duties in February 2024 and has loosened mortgage rules to support prices.

essentials.title: Rates drive affordability
essentials.body: Mortgages are tied to HIBOR or the prime rate, which follow US rates. Rate cuts make buying cheaper.

essentials.title: Developers are powerful
essentials.body: A handful of tycoon-led developers built much of Hong Kong and hold huge land banks.

The city has everything from Michelin three-star Cantonese to HK$40 cha chaan teng sets, and it's going through big changes as people spend more in Shenzhen and many restaurants close. topics.tagline: Wednesday nights at Happy Valley, Sundays at Sha Tin, and the world's richest betting pools.
topics.why: Horse racing is Hong Kong's great shared pastime. The Hong Kong Jockey Club runs some of the best-attended, highest-quality and richest racing in the world, and its betting turnover is enormous. Even people who never bet know the big horses, and an evening at Happy Valley is a classic social night out. Knowing the basics lets you join in at work, at dim sum, and at the track.

essentials.title: The Jockey Club runs everything
essentials.body: The HKJC is a non-profit that holds the legal monopoly on racing, football and lottery betting. It's one of the city's biggest taxpayers and charity donors.

essentials.title: Two racecourses
essentials.body: Happy Valley is the floodlit city-centre track, raced on Wednesday nights. Sha Tin is the big modern course in the New Territories, used mainly on weekends and for international races.

essentials.title: The season
essentials.body: Racing runs from September to July, with a summer break. There are about 88 race meetings a year.

essentials.title: Ratings and handicaps
essentials.body: Horses get a rating, and better horses carry more weight to even out races. Horses move between classes (Class 1 is the best, Class 5 the lowest).

essentials.title: Trainers and jockeys are stars
essentials.body: Only about two dozen licensed trainers and a small group of world-class jockeys compete, so the same names come up every week.

essentials.title: Hong Kong horses are world class
essentials.body: Hong Kong-trained horses regularly win abroad, and the December international races at Sha Tin attract the world's best.

essentials.title: Betting types
essentials.body: Win, Place and Quinella (first two in any order) are the basics. Exotic bets like the Triple Trio can pay millions.

topics.tagline: Indexes, AI stocks, interest rates, and the eternal question: what are you buying?
topics.why: Everyone in Hong Kong has an opinion on the market, from the Hang Seng to US tech stocks. Investing talk is about what's going up, what the central banks will do, and whether something is a bubble. You don't need to give advice; you just need to understand the vocabulary, the big names and the main schools of thought so you can follow along and ask good questions.

essentials.title: Stocks, bonds and funds
essentials.body: A stock is a slice of a company. A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays interest. Funds and ETFs bundle many of them together.

essentials.title: Indexes measure the market
essentials.body: The S&P 500 (500 big US companies), Nasdaq (tech-heavy), Dow Jones, and in Hong Kong the Hang Seng Index (HSI). 'The market is up' usually means one of these.

essentials.title: Interest rates move everything
essentials.body: When central banks like the US Federal Reserve raise rates, borrowing costs rise and stocks often fall. Cuts usually help stocks and property. Hong Kong's rates follow the US because of the currency peg.

essentials.title: Passive vs active
essentials.body: Passive investors buy cheap index funds and hold. Active investors pick stocks or pay managers to try to beat the market, which most fail to do after fees.

essentials.title: The AI trade
essentials.body: Since 2023, a few giant US tech companies, especially Nvidia, have driven much of the market's gains on AI enthusiasm. Whether it's a bubble is the debate of the moment.

essentials.title: Risk and diversification
essentials.body: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across assets and regions reduces the chance of a big loss.

essentials.title: Valuation
essentials.body: The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compares a share price to profits. High P/E means investors expect strong growth, or the stock is expensive.

topics.why: Japanese food is Hong Kong's favourite foreign cuisine, and Japan is the city's favourite holiday destination. People talk about omakase counters, ramen queues, the best wagyu, and where they ate on their last trip to Osaka or Hokkaido. Knowing the main styles, a little etiquette and some vocabulary lets you join these conversations and order with confidence.

essentials.title: Sushi vs sashimi
essentials.body: Sashimi is sliced raw fish on its own. Sushi is anything with vinegared rice: nigiri (fish on rice), maki (rolls) and temaki (hand rolls).

essentials.title: Omakase
essentials.body: 'I leave it to you': the chef serves a set sequence of seasonal dishes at the counter. It's the prestige way to eat sushi, and prices can run to thousands of dollars.

essentials.title: Ramen styles
essentials.body: Tonkotsu (rich pork bone), shoyu (soy), shio (salt) and miso are the main broths. Tsukemen is dipping noodles.

essentials.title: Izakaya culture
essentials.body: Japanese pubs serving small plates, yakitori (grilled skewers) and drinks. Casual and social.

essentials.title: Wagyu and grading
essentials.body: Wagyu is Japanese beef known for marbling. A5 is the top grade; Kobe, Matsusaka and Omi are famous brands.

essentials.title: Kaiseki
essentials.body: A multi-course traditional meal celebrating the season, the haute cuisine of Japan.

essentials.title: Seasonality matters
essentials.body: Japanese cuisine revolves around the seasons: sakura in spring, eel in summer, matsutake mushrooms in autumn, crab and fugu in winter.

topics.tagline: Idols, fandoms, comeback stages and Hong Kong's own pop legends.
topics.why: K-pop is a global cultural force, and Canto-pop is the soundtrack of Hong Kong. Fans follow groups closely, buy albums, attend concerts and debate who's best. In Hong Kong, Canto-pop has had a revival led by boy band MIRROR, while legends like Leslie Cheung and Anita Mui still define the city's culture. Knowing the key names and fan language makes music small talk easy.

essentials.body: Entertainment companies train young 'idols' for years, then debut them in groups with polished choreography. Groups release music in 'comebacks'.

topics.tagline: The Birkin waitlist, the Chanel price hikes, and bags as a currency.
topics.why: Luxury handbags are the core of the fashion business and, for some models, an asset class. A Hermès Birkin can cost more on the resale market than in the store, and Chanel's classic flap has risen in price many times over. In Hong Kong, bags are a highly visible status signal and a big resale industry, so bag talk is everywhere: at work, among friends and on social media.

essentials.title: The hierarchy
essentials.body: Hermès sits at the top, then Chanel. Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine, Loewe, Bottega Veneta, Prada and Goyard follow. Quiet brands like The Row are the connoisseur's choice.

essentials.title: Hermès plays hard to get
essentials.body: You can't simply buy a Birkin or Kelly. Sales associates offer them to clients with a strong purchase history, a practice people call 'the game'.

essentials.title: Classics hold value
essentials.body: Iconic models like the Birkin, Kelly, Chanel Classic Flap and LV Speedy hold value better than seasonal 'it-bags'.

essentials.title: Leathers and hardware matter
essentials.body: Collectors talk about leathers (Togo, Epsom, caviar, lambskin), sizes (Birkin 25, 30, 35) and hardware (gold or palladium).

essentials.title: Resale is a big market
essentials.body: Pre-owned shops and platforms authenticate and resell bags. Condition, box and receipt affect price.

essentials.title: Fakes are a huge issue
essentials.body: 'Superfakes' are hard to spot, which is why authentication services and trusted dealers matter.

topics.tagline: Thirty teams, 82 games, and the most talked-about athletes on social media.
topics.why: The NBA is the world's top basketball league and probably the most global American sport, hugely popular across Asia. Its stars are celebrities on and off the court, and fans argue endlessly about who's the greatest, which trades make sense, and whether the league is better than it used to be. You can follow it casually through highlights, which come out during Hong Kong mornings.

essentials.title: League structure
essentials.body: 30 teams split into the Eastern and Western Conferences. Each plays 82 regular-season games from October to April.

essentials.title: The playoffs are what matters
essentials.body: Sixteen teams make the playoffs (with a 'play-in' for seeds 7 to 10). Every round is best-of-seven, ending in the NBA Finals in June. A ring (championship) defines legacies.

essentials.title: Stars move a lot
essentials.body: Unlike football clubs, NBA stars often switch teams through trades and free agency. Superteams and blockbuster trades are constant talking points.

essentials.title: Salary cap and the draft
essentials.body: A salary cap and luxury tax limit spending. The worst teams get the best chance at top picks in the annual draft, so bad teams sometimes 'tank' on purpose.

essentials.title: Stats rule the conversation
essentials.body: Points, rebounds and assists per game, plus shooting percentages. A 'triple-double' is 10 or more in three categories in one game.

essentials.title: The GOAT debate never ends
essentials.body: Michael Jordan vs LeBron James is the eternal argument. Knowing both sides is half of NBA small talk.

topics.tagline: Twenty clubs, 38 games each, and the most-watched league on the planet.
topics.why: The Premier League is England's top football division and the most popular sports league in the world, watched in almost every country. In Hong Kong it's the default sports small talk: people stay up for 10pm, midnight and 3am kick-offs and support a club for life, often one they picked as a kid in the 1990s or 2000s. You don't need to know tactics. Knowing which club someone supports, how that club is doing, and a few big names gets you a long way.

essentials.title: How the season works
essentials.body: It runs August to May. Each of the 20 clubs plays every other club twice, home and away: 38 games. A win is 3 points, a draw 1, a loss 0. Most points wins the title. There are no playoffs for the title.

essentials.title: Relegation makes the bottom exciting
essentials.body: The bottom three clubs drop down to the Championship (the second tier) and three clubs come up. Staying up is worth well over £100 million, so the relegation fight is as tense as the title race.

essentials.title: Europe is the other prize
essentials.body: Finishing in the top four or five gets a club into next season's Champions League, Europe's elite club competition, which brings money and prestige. Lower places can mean the Europa League or Conference League.

essentials.title: The 'Big Six'

essentials.title: There are other trophies too
essentials.body: The FA Cup is the oldest knockout cup in the world (since 1871) and includes amateur sides. The League Cup (Carabao Cup) is the smaller domestic cup. Winning several in one season is a 'double' or 'treble'.

essentials.title: Managers and money drive everything
essentials.body: Clubs live and die by their manager (head coach) and transfer spending. Two transfer windows, summer and January, are when players are bought and sold, and the gossip around them is a sport of its own.

essentials.title: It's tribal
essentials.body: Fans support one club, often inherited, and rivalries are deep: Liverpool vs Manchester United, Arsenal vs Tottenham (the North London derby), City vs United (the Manchester derby). Asking 'who do you support?' is the universal opener.

People compare iPhones and Androids, cameras and batteries, and talk about new launches like foldables and AI features. topics.tagline: Rubber, hype and limited drops: why people queue overnight for shoes.
topics.why: Sneaker culture turned sports shoes into collectibles, fashion statements and an investment market. It's tied to basketball, hip-hop, skateboarding and streetwear, and a few brands release limited models that sell out in seconds and resell for many times their price. Hong Kong has a famous sneaker street and a strong streetwear scene, so shoes are an easy, fun topic.

essentials.title: Drops and hype
essentials.body: Brands release limited 'drops' through apps and raffles. Demand far exceeds supply, so shoes resell above retail on platforms like StockX and GOAT.

essentials.title: Nike rules, but it's shifting
essentials.body: Nike (with Jordan Brand) dominates. But in the 2020s, running brands like On and Hoka and retro styles from Adidas and New Balance have stolen attention.

essentials.title: Collaborations drive heat
essentials.body: Collabs with designers and celebrities, like Travis Scott, Off-White's Virgil Abloh, or Sacai, create the most wanted shoes.

essentials.title: Silhouettes are the models
essentials.body: Collectors talk in silhouettes: Air Jordan 1, Air Force 1, Dunk, Air Max, Yeezy Boost, Samba, 550. Each has many colourways.

essentials.title: Condition is everything
essentials.body: 'Deadstock' (unworn) shoes in the original box hold value. Worn ones drop sharply.

essentials.title: Trends cycle fast
essentials.body: Chunky 'dad shoes', then slim terrace shoes like the Adidas Samba, then running shoes as fashion. What's hot changes every year or two.

topics.tagline: Four Grand Slams, one long season, and a new rivalry after the golden era.
topics.why: Tennis is a global individual sport with a year-round tour, and its biggest events (the four Grand Slams) are cultural moments. After two decades of Federer, Nadal and Djokovic, a new generation led by Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has taken over. It's an easy sport to talk about because the storylines are personal: rivalries, comebacks, ageing champions and rising stars.

essentials.title: The four Grand Slams
essentials.body: Australian Open (January, hard court), French Open or Roland Garros (May-June, clay), Wimbledon (July, grass) and the US Open (August-September, hard court). Slam titles are how careers are measured.

essentials.title: Surfaces change everything
essentials.body: Clay is slow with high bounces, rewarding grinders like Nadal. Grass is fast and low, rewarding big serves. Hard courts sit in between. Players often have a favourite surface.

essentials.title: Scoring is weird
essentials.body: Points go 15, 30, 40, game. 'Love' means zero, 'deuce' is 40-40. Six games win a set (by two), with a tiebreak at 6-6. Men play best-of-five sets at Slams; women best-of-three.

essentials.title: Two tours
essentials.body: The ATP runs men's tennis and the WTA runs women's. Players earn ranking points; the world number one is a big deal.

essentials.title: The Big Three era is over
essentials.body: Federer (20 Slams), Nadal (22) and Djokovic (24, the record) dominated from 2003 onward. Federer retired in 2022, Nadal in 2024, and Djokovic is in his late thirties.

essentials.title: Sinner vs Alcaraz
essentials.body: The two young stars split all eight Slams in 2024 and 2025 between them. Their matches, including the epic 2025 French Open final, are the new must-watch rivalry.

essentials.body: When prices rise fast (inflation), central banks raise rates to cool demand. When the economy slows, they cut. The US Fed's moves ripple worldwide.

topics.tagline: Little machines that tell time worse than your phone, and why people pay a fortune for them.
topics.why: Fine watches are one of the few accessories people wear as a quiet signal: of taste, success, or nerdy appreciation for tiny engineering. A mechanical watch is a few hundred hand-finished parts with no battery. Watch talk is really about history, craftsmanship, design icons and the hype around models you can't simply walk in and buy. Hong Kong is one of the world's biggest watch markets, so it comes up constantly.

essentials.title: Mechanical vs quartz
essentials.body: Quartz watches run on a battery and are more accurate. Mechanical watches run on a wound spring, and enthusiasts love them precisely because they're old-school craftsmanship.

essentials.title: The movement is the engine
essentials.body: The movement (or calibre) is the mechanism inside. 'In-house' means the brand makes its own, which carries prestige. Many good brands use reliable movements from suppliers like ETA or Sellita.

essentials.title: Complications are extra functions
essentials.body: Anything beyond hours, minutes and seconds: date, chronograph (stopwatch), GMT (second time zone), moon phase, perpetual calendar, tourbillon, minute repeater. More complications, more cost.

essentials.title: The holy trinity
essentials.body: Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin are seen as the top tier of traditional Swiss watchmaking.

essentials.title: Steel sports watches are the hype
essentials.body: Rolex Submariner, GMT-Master II and Daytona, AP Royal Oak, Patek Nautilus. Demand outstrips supply, so there are waitlists, purchase histories and resale prices above retail.

essentials.title: Watch categories
essentials.body: Dive watches, pilot watches, chronographs, dress watches, GMTs and 'integrated bracelet' sports watches. Knowing the category helps you compliment someone's choice.

essentials.title: Price tiers
essentials.body: Roughly: Seiko, Tissot, Hamilton under HK$10,000; Tudor, Longines, Oris and Omega in the tens of thousands; Rolex upward; the trinity and independents into the hundreds of thousands and beyond.

topics.tagline: Peat, casks and age statements: the language of the world's most collected spirit.
topics.why: Whisky is a favourite of business dinners, bars and gift-giving in Hong Kong, where Macallan and Japanese whisky are status symbols. Whisky lovers talk about regions, cask types, age and smoky 'peat', and many collect rare bottles. Learn the main styles and a few distilleries and you can order well, appreciate a gift, and enjoy a conversation at the bar.

essentials.title: Whisky vs whiskey
essentials.body: Scotland, Japan and Canada spell it 'whisky'; Ireland and the US usually use 'whiskey'.

essentials.title: Single malt vs blended
essentials.body: Single malt is made from malted barley at one distillery. Blended whisky mixes malts and grain whisky, like Johnnie Walker. Single malts are the connoisseur's focus.

essentials.title: Scotland's regions
essentials.body: Speyside (fruity, elegant: Macallan, Glenfiddich), Islay (smoky, peaty: Laphroaig, Lagavulin, Ardbeg), Highlands (varied), Lowlands (light) and Campbeltown (briny).

essentials.title: Casks shape flavour
essentials.body: Most flavour comes from the oak barrel. Ex-bourbon casks give vanilla; sherry casks give dried fruit and spice.

essentials.title: Age statements
essentials.body: A 12-year-old whisky spent at least 12 years in the cask. Older isn't always better, but it's rarer and pricier.

essentials.title: American whiskey
essentials.body: Bourbon must be mostly corn and aged in new charred oak, giving sweet caramel notes. Rye is spicier.

essentials.title: Japanese whisky
essentials.body: Modelled on Scotch but famously refined; Yamazaki and Hibiki became so popular that age-statement bottles ran short.

topics.tagline: Grapes, places and vintages: how to order, taste and talk without sounding lost.
topics.why: Wine is the default drink at business dinners, weddings and celebrations in Hong Kong, which became Asia's wine hub after scrapping wine duty in 2008. Wine talk can feel intimidating, but it rests on a few ideas: grape varieties, regions, vintages and how a wine tastes. Learn those and you can order confidently, compliment the host's bottle, and ask the questions that get wine lovers talking.

essentials.title: Grapes vs places
essentials.body: New World wines (Australia, US, Chile, NZ) are usually labelled by grape, like 'Cabernet Sauvignon'. Old World wines (France, Italy, Spain) are labelled by place, like 'Bordeaux', and you're expected to know which grapes grow there.

essentials.title: The big red grapes
essentials.body: Cabernet Sauvignon (bold, structured), Merlot (softer), Pinot Noir (light, elegant), Syrah/Shiraz (spicy), plus Italy's Nebbiolo and Sangiovese and Spain's Tempranillo.

essentials.title: The big white grapes
essentials.body: Chardonnay (from crisp to buttery), Sauvignon Blanc (zesty), Riesling (aromatic, can be sweet or dry), plus Pinot Grigio and Chenin Blanc.

essentials.title: France's key regions
essentials.body: Bordeaux (Cabernet and Merlot blends; the 'first growths'), Burgundy (Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; tiny prestigious plots), Champagne (sparkling), the Rhône (Syrah, Grenache) and the Loire.

essentials.title: How tasting works
essentials.body: Look, swirl, smell, sip. People describe body (light to full), acidity, tannin (the drying feel in reds), sweetness and finish (how long the taste lasts).

essentials.title: Vintage matters, sometimes
essentials.body: The vintage is the year the grapes were picked. Weather makes some years better, which matters most for top Bordeaux, Burgundy and Champagne.

essentials.title: Food pairing basics
essentials.body: Match weight with weight: big reds with steak, crisp whites with seafood, off-dry Riesling with spicy food, Champagne with almost anything fried or salty, including dim sum.
